en.title: Nutrition and Dietetics: the whole course
en.short: What nutrition and dietetics is, how the course is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text: These notes teach concepts in nutrition and dietetics to students. They are not medical advice and do not replace your teachers, textbooks, clinical supervisors or official guidance. They do not give drug doses. Clinical guidelines change and differ between countries, so check the current national guidance or World Health Organization (WHO) source before you apply anything to a patient. Anyone who is unwell should seek local clinical help.

sections.heading: What nutrition and dietetics is
sections.text:
Nutrition is the science of how food supplies energy and nutrients, how the body uses them, and how diet affects health and disease. Dietetics is the professional use of that science to assess a person, plan food and nutrition care, and support change in real settings. It draws on biology, chemistry, food science, physiology, psychology, sociology and public health.

A nutritionist and a dietitian are not always the same role. The title dietitian is usually protected and tied to registration, while nutritionist is used more widely and its meaning varies by country. Check the rules where you plan to work.

sections.heading: How the course is usually organised
sections.text:
Awards and lengths differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, universities commonly offer BSc Nutrition and Dietetics or Human Nutrition and Dietetics, and some polytechnics offer diploma and higher diploma routes in related fields. In the UK, an approved degree plus supervised practice leads to registration as a dietitian, regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). In the United States, the registered dietitian (RD) credential, formerly registered dietitian nutritionist (RDN), is administered through the Commission on Dietetic Registration.

Most programmes combine basic science, food science, community nutrition, clinical nutrition, food service management, professional practice and a project or placement. Entry requirements, course length, registration and licensure rules change, so check your own handbook and national regulator.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introduction stage starts with concepts and professions, then macronutrients, micronutrients, digestion, absorption and metabolism, energy balance and requirements, foods and food groups, food processing, nutrition calculations and measurement, and food culture, eating behaviour and food security. These give the vocabulary and quantitative base for later work.

The core stage moves from assessment to action. Students learn nutritional assessment; dietary standards and food-based dietary guidelines; nutrition through the life cycle, from maternal and infant nutrition to child, adolescent, adult and older adult nutrition; undernutrition and micronutrient deficiencies; obesity and weight management; and nutrition therapy in diabetes, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, gastrointestinal, liver and allergic disease, and cancer, HIV and palliative care. Clinical nutrition support, public health nutrition, nutrition education and counselling, food service systems and management, professional practice, ethics and law, and research methods complete the core.

At master’s level, advanced nutrition science, nutritional epidemiology, nutrition policy and food systems, and advanced research methods and dissertation deepen these themes. The order can vary, but the logic is usually normal nutrition first, then assessment, then disease and public health, then professional and research skills.

sections.heading: How to study nutrition and dietetics
sections.text:
Learn the normal first. Know what each nutrient does, where it is found, how it is digested and absorbed, and what happens when it is missing or excessive. Then link that knowledge to assessment and to particular groups or diseases. For calculations, write the units at every step and check that the answer is plausible. A negative energy intake or impossible body mass index usually means a unit error.

Use active recall and spaced practice. Draw digestion and metabolic pathways from memory. Practise dietary calculations, food exchange lists and case questions. Read food labels and dietary guidelines with care. In clinical topics, learn the questions to ask and the safety checks, not just lists of foods to avoid. Keep a notebook of cases and corrections.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
Students memorise nutrient lists without function or context, so they cannot reason about a new case. Others confuse nutritionist and dietitian, or quote one country’s guideline as universal. In calculations, mixing units such as kilojoules and kilocalories, grams and milligrams, or daily and weekly values is common. Some give general advice as a prescription, without assessment, consent or cultural context.

Another mistake is treating these notes as medical advice. Clinical decisions need a qualified clinician who can assess the person and check current national or WHO guidance. Learn to say what you know, what you do not know, and when to refer.

keyPoints: Nutrition is the science of food, nutrients and health; dietetics is its professional use in assessment and care.
The course usually moves from normal nutrition and nutrients to assessment, disease, public health and professional practice.
Degree names, lengths, registration and licensure differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook and regulator.
Learn normal function first, then link it to assessment, disease and practical calculations.
Use active recall, spaced practice and worked calculations rather than rereading alone.
These notes teach concepts and are not medical advice; check current national or WHO guidance for clinical decisions.

en.title: Nutrition and dietetics: concepts and professions
en.short: Core terms, scope, careers, regulation and history of nutrition and dietetics.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.text: Food is any substance eaten to supply energy and nutrients. Nutrients are the chemicals in food used for energy, growth, repair and regulation. Diet means a person’s usual pattern of foods and drinks, not only a weight-loss plan. Nutrition is the science of nutrients, how the body uses them, and the factors that affect need and status. Malnutrition is poor nutrition in any form: undernutrition, overnutrition, or micronutrient (vitamin and mineral) deficiency. Dietetics is the practical use of nutrition science to plan food and feeding for individuals and groups in health and disease.

sections.heading: Scope and practice
sections.text: Nutrition science studies nutrients, requirements, food composition, assessment and the links between diet and health. Dietetic practice applies this knowledge through assessment, diagnosis of nutrition problems, planning, counselling, food service and monitoring. A dietitian usually works in hospitals, clinics, community programmes, food services or research. A nutritionist may do similar work, but titles and legal protection vary. Case: Amina, a community nutrition officer in Kano, finds a thin child and an adult with high blood pressure. Both need assessment, advice and referral; she does not give drug treatment.

sections.heading: Careers and regulation
sections.text: Career paths include clinical dietetics, public health nutrition, food service management, nutrition education, research, food industry and policy. Regulation differs by country. In the United Kingdom, dietitians must register with the Health and Care Professions Council to use the protected title. In the United States, the registered dietitian nutritionist credential comes from the Commission on Dietetic Registration, and state licensure varies. Some countries regulate through a national council or association; others have little statutory control. Check current national rules before using a title or practising.

sections.heading: History and agencies
sections.text: Modern nutrition grew in the early 1900s, when vitamins were shown to prevent diseases such as scurvy and beriberi. FAO, founded in 1945, works on food security and nutrition. WHO, founded in 1948, gives global nutrition guidance and monitors malnutrition.

keyPoints: Food supplies energy and nutrients; diet is a person’s usual eating pattern.
Nutrition is the science of nutrients and their use; dietetics applies it to feeding people.
Malnutrition includes undernutrition, overnutrition and micronutrient deficiency.
Career paths include clinical dietetics, public health, food service, education, research and policy.
Dietitian titles and registration are regulated differently by country, so check current national rules.
Vitamins were discovered in the early 1900s; FAO and WHO lead international nutrition work.

en.title: Macronutrients: carbohydrates, proteins and fats
en.short: Carbohydrate, protein and fat structure, sources, energy yields, quality, fibre and life-course needs.

sections.heading: Classes and structure
sections.text: Carbohydrates are sugars, starches and fibre. Monosaccharides are single sugars such as glucose. Disaccharides are two sugars, such as sucrose. Polysaccharides are long chains, such as starch and glycogen. Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; they build tissues and act as enzymes and hormones. Dietary fats are mostly triglycerides: one glycerol with three fatty acids. They store energy and cushion organs. Phospholipids, another type of lipid, form cell membranes. Fatty acids are saturated, monounsaturated or polyunsaturated, and may be cis or trans.

sections.heading: Energy and sources
sections.text:
Using Atwater factors, carbohydrate and protein supply about 4 kcal per gram, and fat about 9 kcal per gram. For example, a meal with 60 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein and 15 g fat gives:
60 × 4 = 240 kcal
20 × 4 = 80 kcal
15 × 9 = 135 kcal
Total = 455 kcal.
Staples such as rice, maize, cassava and bread supply carbohydrate. Legumes, fish, eggs, meat and milk supply protein. Oils, nuts, seeds, butter and fatty meat supply fat.

sections.heading: Quality and essentials
sections.text: Nine amino acids are essential for adults: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine. Protein quality depends on essential amino acid pattern and digestibility. A limiting amino acid is the one in shortest supply. Cereals are often low in lysine; legumes are low in methionine, so combining them improves quality. Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are essential fatty acids. They must come from foods such as vegetable oils, nuts and seeds.

sections.heading: Fibre and life course
sections.text: Dietary fibre is plant material resistant to human digestion, mainly non-starch polysaccharides and lignin. It aids bowel function and may lower disease risk. Requirements for energy and protein change with age, sex, pregnancy, lactation and activity; check current national or WHO guidance. Inadequate protein and energy intake causes protein-energy malnutrition, especially in young children. Excess energy from any macronutrient is stored as fat. Excess saturated fat and added sugar raise obesity and heart disease risk. High fibre needs enough fluid.

keyPoints: Carbohydrate and protein yield about 4 kcal/g; fat yields about 9 kcal/g.
Monosaccharides are single sugars, disaccharides two sugars, and polysaccharides long chains such as starch.
Proteins are amino acid chains; nine amino acids are essential for adults.
Protein quality depends on essential amino acid pattern and digestibility; cereals and legumes complement each other.
Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are essential fatty acids.
Dietary fibre is plant material resistant to human digestion, mainly non-starch polysaccharides and lignin.

en.title: Micronutrients: vitamins and minerals
en.short: Fat- and water-soluble vitamins, major minerals and trace elements: functions, sources, deficiency and toxicity.

sections.heading: Two classes of vitamins
sections.text: Vitamins are organic compounds needed in small amounts. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) dissolve in fat, are absorbed with dietary fat, and are stored in the liver and fatty tissue. Fat malabsorption or a very low-fat diet therefore reduces uptake. Water-soluble vitamins (vitamin C and the B group) dissolve in water; most are not stored in large amounts, so excess passes in urine and regular intake matters more. Vitamin B12 is an exception: the liver stores several years’ worth.

sections.heading: Minerals and bioavailability
sections.text: Minerals are inorganic elements. Major minerals (calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, sodium, potassium, chloride and sulfur) are needed in grams or hundreds of milligrams daily; trace elements such as iron, zinc, iodine, selenium, copper and fluoride in milligrams or micrograms. Bioavailability is the share of a nutrient eaten that is absorbed and used. It depends on the food and the meal. Haem iron from meat is better absorbed than non-haem iron from plants. Vitamin C taken with a meal raises non-haem iron absorption; phytates in cereals and tannins in tea lower it.

sections.heading: Deficiency, toxicity and needs
sections.text:
Deficiency appears when intake, absorption or need is out of balance; toxicity when intake is too high. Fat-soluble vitamins accumulate, so very high vitamin A can damage the liver and cause birth defects, and excess vitamin D raises blood calcium. Water-soluble vitamins are safer but not risk-free.

Requirements differ with age, sex, pregnancy, lactation and disease. Case: a young woman eats mainly maize and drinks tea with meals. Her iron intake looks adequate on paper, but phytates and tannins reduce absorption. Adding a vitamin C source and moving tea away from meals improves uptake without changing the iron eaten.

keyPoints: Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are stored; water-soluble ones are largely excreted.
Bioavailability is the fraction of a nutrient absorbed and used.
Haem iron is better absorbed than non-haem iron; vitamin C helps, phytates and tannins hinder.
Fat-soluble vitamins are more prone to toxicity because they accumulate.
Requirements vary with age, sex, pregnancy, lactation and disease.
Check current national or WHO guidance for recommended intakes.

en.title: Digestion, absorption and metabolism
en.short: How the gut digests food, absorbs nutrients and routes them into metabolism.

sections.heading: Gut anatomy and secretions
sections.text:
The gastrointestinal tract includes the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), large intestine and rectum. Accessory organs are salivary glands, pancreas, liver and gallbladder. Villi and microvilli make the small intestine the main site of digestion and absorption.

Secretion is controlled by nerves and hormones. Saliva contains amylase and mucus. The stomach secretes hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen and mucus. The pancreas secretes enzymes and bicarbonate, which neutralises acid. The liver makes bile, stored in the gallbladder; bile salts emulsify fat. Intestinal enzymes finish digestion at the brush border, the surface formed by microvilli.

sections.heading: Mechanical and chemical digestion
sections.text: Mechanical digestion is physical breakdown: chewing, stomach churning, segmentation (mixing contractions) and peristalsis. Chemical digestion uses enzymes to hydrolyse bonds. Carbohydrates become monosaccharides, proteins become amino acids and small peptides, and fats become fatty acids and monoglycerides. Enzymes work at specific pH: gastric pepsin needs acid, while pancreatic enzymes need alkaline conditions.

sections.heading: Absorption and transport
sections.text: Absorption moves nutrients across the intestinal wall. Mechanisms include passive diffusion, facilitated diffusion, active transport and endocytosis. Monosaccharides and amino acids enter capillaries and travel in the portal vein to the liver. Long-chain fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins are packaged into chylomicrons, lipoprotein particles that enter lymph and then blood. Water and electrolytes are absorbed mainly in the small and large intestine.

sections.heading: Metabolism and bioavailability
sections.text:
Metabolism is all chemical reactions in cells. Catabolism breaks molecules down and releases energy, some of which is captured as ATP (cell energy). Anabolism builds molecules and uses ATP. The liver stores glycogen, makes glucose, forms urea, produces bile and plasma proteins, and detoxifies substances. Absorbed glucose may be used for energy or stored; amino acids build proteins or are broken down; fatty acids are used for energy or stored.

Bioavailability is the proportion of a nutrient absorbed and available for use. It varies with food form, processing, cooking, fibre, phytates, oxalates, nutrient interactions, gut health and drugs. For example, vitamin C in an orange eaten with maize and beans can increase non-haem iron absorption (the iron in plant foods), while phytate in the maize and beans reduces it.

keyPoints: The small intestine is the main site of digestion and absorption because villi and microvilli increase surface area.
Mechanical digestion breaks food physically; chemical digestion uses enzymes to hydrolyse nutrients.
Absorption uses passive diffusion, facilitated diffusion, active transport and endocytosis.
Water-soluble nutrients travel in the portal vein to the liver, while long-chain fats enter chylomicrons and lymph.
Catabolism releases energy captured as ATP and anabolism uses ATP; the liver stores glycogen, makes glucose, forms urea and detoxifies substances.
Bioavailability depends on food form, processing, fibre, phytates, nutrient interactions, gut health and drugs.

en.title: Energy, energy balance and requirements
en.short: This summary covers energy units, Atwater factors, expenditure, requirement estimates and energy balance with calculations.

sections.heading: Energy units and Atwater factors
sections.text: Energy is measured in kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal). 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ; 1 kJ = 0.239 kcal. Food energy is metabolisable energy. Atwater factors estimate it: carbohydrate 4 kcal/g (17 kJ/g), protein 4 kcal/g (17 kJ/g), fat 9 kcal/g (37 kJ/g), alcohol 7 kcal/g (29 kJ/g). These are averages; fibre and food processing change actual values. Worked example: a meal has 60 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein and 15 g fat. Energy = (60×4)+(20×4)+(15×9)=240+80+135=455 kcal. In kJ = (60×17)+(20×17)+(15×37)=1020+340+555=1915 kJ, about 1,920 kJ.

sections.heading: Components of expenditure
sections.text: Total energy expenditure has three main parts. Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is energy for vital functions measured at rest after fasting and sleep. Resting metabolic rate (RMR) is similar but measured less strictly and is slightly higher. BMR is the largest part, often 60 to 70 percent. Thermic effect of food (TEF) is energy used to digest, absorb and metabolise nutrients, about 10 percent of intake. Physical activity is the most variable part. Physical activity level (PAL) is a multiplier applied to BMR or RMR to estimate total expenditure.

sections.heading: Estimating requirements
sections.text: Energy requirement is the intake that balances expenditure and supports growth. Requirements are estimated from measured expenditure, predictive equations or dietary reference values. Predictive equations use age, sex, weight and height to estimate BMR or RMR; the result is multiplied by a PAL. For groups, the factorial method adds BMR, TEF and activity. Equations are estimates only, so use current WHO or national guidance for individuals.

sections.heading: Energy balance and weight
sections.text: Energy balance is intake minus expenditure. If intake equals expenditure, weight is stable. A positive balance stores energy, mostly as fat; a negative balance uses stores. A common approximation is 1 kg body fat = 7,700 kcal (about 32,000 kJ), but this varies. Worked example: intake 2,500 kcal/day and expenditure 2,300 kcal/day give a surplus of 200 kcal/day. Over 30 days: 200×30=6,000 kcal; 6,000÷7,700=0.78 kg, about 0.8 kg fat if all surplus is stored.

keyPoints: 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.
Atwater factors: carbohydrate 4 kcal/g, protein 4 kcal/g, fat 9 kcal/g, alcohol 7 kcal/g.
Total energy expenditure = BMR or RMR + thermic effect of food + physical activity.
Energy requirement is the intake that balances expenditure and supports growth.
Energy balance = intake − expenditure; positive balance stores energy and negative balance uses it.
A surplus or deficit of 7,700 kcal is often taken as about 1 kg body fat, but this is an approximation.

en.title: Foods, food groups and food processing
en.short: Food groups, composition tables, labels, processing effects and basic food safety.

sections.heading: Food groups
sections.text: Food groups are sets of foods with similar nutrient roles. Common groups are staples, such as cereals, roots and tubers; legumes, such as beans and groundnuts; vegetables; fruits; animal foods, such as meat, fish, eggs and milk; and fats and sugars. The exact groups differ between countries and food-based dietary guidelines. A staple is the energy-giving food eaten most days. Legumes are seeds of the pea family, rich in protein and fibre. Grouping helps plan varied diets.

sections.heading: Composition and labels
sections.text: A food composition table or database lists nutrients in foods per 100 g edible portion. Check whether values are raw or cooked, and whether waste is included. Values vary with variety, soil, storage and cooking, so use a current national table. Suppose a table gives 8 mg vitamin C per 100 g and a person eats 150 g. Intake is 8 × 150 ÷ 100 = 12 mg. Food labels list ingredients, nutrients, allergens and dates. Label rules differ by country; Codex Alimentarius gives international guidance, and national regulators enforce law.

sections.heading: Processing and preservation
sections.text: Processing is any treatment from harvest to plate. Preservation slows spoilage. Milling removes bran and germ, lowering fibre and some B vitamins and minerals. Heating destroys heat-sensitive vitamins, especially vitamin C and thiamin. Canning and blanching can leach water-soluble vitamins into liquid. Freezing retains nutrients well. Drying, salting and smoking preserve food but may reduce some vitamins. Fermentation can improve digestibility and may add B vitamins. Fortification adds nutrients. Processing also improves safety.

sections.heading: Food safety
sections.text: Basic food safety protects people from foodborne illness. WHO’s Five Keys are: keep clean; separate raw and cooked food; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; and use safe water and raw materials. Wash hands and surfaces, avoid cross-contamination, and refrigerate leftovers promptly. In warm, humid places, store grains and nuts dry to prevent moulds that produce aflatoxins. For outbreaks or clinical advice, follow current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Food groups organise foods by nutrient role, and the exact groups differ between countries.
A food composition table or database lists nutrients per 100 g edible portion; check whether values are raw or cooked.
Nutrient intake from a portion = value per 100 g × portion in g ÷ 100.
Processing can improve safety and digestibility but may remove heat-sensitive vitamins and fibre.
Food labels give ingredients, nutrients, allergens and dates, and label rules differ by country.
Basic food safety follows WHO’s Five Keys, and dry storage of grains and nuts helps prevent aflatoxins.

en.title: Nutrition calculations and measurement
en.short: Unit conversion, dilution, recipe yield, nutrient tables and BMI, with worked examples.

sections.heading: Units and conversions
sections.text: Nutrition uses metric units. Mass: 1 kilogram (kg) = 1000 grams (g); 1 g = 1000 milligrams (mg); 1 mg = 1000 micrograms. Volume: 1 litre (L) = 1000 millilitres (mL). Energy is in kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal); 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ. Convert by multiplying or dividing by 1000, or by using the energy factor. Example: 250 mg = 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.25 g. Always write the unit and check that the answer is sensible.

sections.heading: Percentages and dilution
sections.text: Percentage means parts per 100. A 5% (w/v) solution has 5 g of solute in 100 mL. To dilute, use C1 × V1 = C2 × V2, where C is concentration and V is volume. Example: to make 500 mL of 2% solution from 10% stock, V1 = (2 × 500) ÷ 10 = 100 mL stock, made up to 500 mL with solvent. Check: 100 mL of 10% contains 10 g; 10 g in 500 mL is 2%.

sections.heading: Recipe yield and portions
sections.text: Recipe yield is the amount a recipe makes. If a recipe serves 4 and you need 10 portions, scale by 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5. Ingredient amounts and total weight are multiplied by 2.5. Portion size is total edible weight divided by number of portions. Example: 2.5 kg of stew for 10 portions gives 250 g per portion. Cooking losses, such as water evaporation, change final weight, so weigh after cooking when possible.

sections.heading: Nutrients and anthropometry
sections.text: Anthropometry means measuring the body, such as height and weight. Food composition tables list nutrient content per 100 g edible portion. Nutrient intake = (amount eaten ÷ 100) × table value. Example: 150 g milk with about 120 mg calcium per 100 g gives 1.5 × 120 = 180 mg. Body mass index (BMI) = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². Example: 70 kg and 1.75 m gives 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.9 kg/m². Interpret BMI using age-specific cut-offs; WHO categories are not valid for children or pregnancy. Tables and cut-offs vary by country, so use current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: 1 kg = 1000 g; 1 g = 1000 mg; 1 mg = 1000 micrograms; 1 L = 1000 mL; 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.
Percentage concentration means grams or millilitres per 100 mL or 100 g; dilution uses C1 × V1 = C2 × V2.
Scale a recipe by required portions ÷ recipe portions, then divide total edible weight by portions to get portion size.
Nutrient intake = (amount eaten ÷ 100) × nutrient value per 100 g from a food composition table.
BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²; interpret it with the correct age and population cut-offs.
Use current national or WHO food composition tables and growth references, because values and cut-offs vary.

en.title: Food culture, eating behaviour and household food security
en.short: How culture, religion, income, appetite and household food security shape food choice and practical nutrition advice.

sections.heading: Culture and economy
sections.text:
Food choice is shaped by social, cultural, religious and economic factors. Social factors include family, peers and household roles. Culture gives familiar tastes and meanings. Religion sets rules such as halal, kosher or fasting; practice varies. Income, food prices, transport and time decide what is possible. People often choose foods that are affordable, available and socially acceptable, not only healthy ones.

Food habits are repeated behaviours learned in a family or community. A food taboo is a strong cultural or religious rule against eating a food. Taboos vary and are not all harmful, but avoiding a nutritious food can lower nutrient intake, especially in pregnancy or childhood. Ask about beliefs respectfully and offer acceptable alternatives.

sections.heading: Appetite and behaviour
sections.text:
Appetite is the desire to eat. It is influenced by hunger hormones, mood, stress, sleep, illness and social cues. Satiety is the feeling of fullness that stops eating. Eating behaviour includes meal timing, portion size, snacking, emotional eating and cultural rules. It is not simply willpower. In counselling, explore triggers and routines, then agree small realistic changes.

Case: Amina meets a man who eats large snacks late at night when stressed. She asks when the urge occurs and helps him plan fruit or water at those times and a regular evening meal.

sections.heading: Household food security
sections.text:
Household food security means all members have reliable access to enough nutritious food for an active life. Its dimensions are availability, access, utilisation and stability. Food insecurity ranges from worry about running out to skipping meals. Measurement uses experience scales such as the Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES) and the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale (HFIAS), dietary diversity scores, coping strategy indices and food expenditure. No single measure is perfect; use validated tools and current national or FAO guidance.

Realistic advice considers budget, storage, cooking fuel, market access and who eats first. If food insecurity is found, counsel on affordable local foods and refer to social support where available.

keyPoints: Food choice is shaped by social, cultural, religious and economic factors, not knowledge alone.
Food habits are learned; taboos vary and should be explored respectfully, not dismissed.
Appetite and eating behaviour are influenced by hormones, mood, stress, sleep, illness and social cues.
Household food security means reliable access to enough nutritious food for all members.
Food insecurity is measured with experience scales, dietary diversity, coping strategies and expenditure; no single tool is perfect.
Realistic nutrition advice fits local foods, beliefs and budgets, and refers people to social support when food insecurity is found.

en.title: Nutritional assessment
en.short: The anthropometric, biochemical, clinical and dietary methods used to assess nutritional status.

sections.heading: The ABCD model
sections.text:
Nutritional assessment gathers evidence from four streams: anthropometric (body size and composition), biochemical (laboratory tests), clinical (history and physical signs) and dietary (food and nutrient intake). This is the ABCD model. Each stream answers a different question and each has error.

Assessment is not diagnosis. Interpret findings together, using appropriate reference data and the person’s age, sex, pregnancy, illness and setting. Guidelines change, so follow current WHO or national guidance.

sections.heading: Anthropometry
sections.text:
Height and weight need calibrated equipment. BMI = weight in kilograms ÷ height in metres squared. It screens for underweight or overweight but does not measure body fat. Example: 68 kg and 1.62 m give 1.62 × 1.62 = 2.6244, so BMI = 68 ÷ 2.6244 = 25.9 kg/m².

Waist circumference indicates central fat; cutoffs vary by population. Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a quick measure used in children and pregnant women. Skinfolds estimate subcutaneous fat but need trained observers and population-specific equations.

sections.heading: Biochemical and clinical
sections.text:
Biochemical tests include haemoglobin, ferritin, vitamin and mineral markers, and blood glucose or lipids where relevant. Interpret results with inflammation, hydration, kidney function and laboratory reference ranges, because many markers change in illness.

Clinical assessment covers medical and diet history, medicines, weight change, appetite, swallowing, and signs such as oedema, wasting, hair and skin changes. Signs are often non-specific, so clinical findings support other measures.

sections.heading: Dietary methods and validity
sections.text:
A 24-hour recall asks what was eaten in the past day. It is quick but depends on memory and may not represent usual intake. A food frequency questionnaire asks how often foods are eaten over a period; it captures usual patterns but is limited by a fixed food list. A weighed record measures foods as eaten, often over several days; it is detailed but burdensome and may change eating.

Validity is whether a method measures what it claims; reliability is whether it gives consistent results. Combine methods, and check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: The ABCD model covers anthropometric, biochemical, clinical and dietary evidence.
BMI = weight in kilograms ÷ height in metres squared; it is a screening measure, not a diagnosis.
Waist circumference, MUAC and skinfolds add information but need population-appropriate references and training.
Biochemical results must be read with illness, hydration and local reference ranges.
Dietary methods differ in validity: 24-hour recall, food frequency questionnaire and weighed record each have strengths and limitations.
Combine methods and use current WHO or national guidance.

en.title: Dietary standards and food-based dietary guidelines
en.short: Nutrient reference values, food-based guidelines and front-of-pack labels: how standards guide dietary advice.

sections.heading: Reference values
sections.text:
Nutrient reference values are numerical benchmarks for assessing and planning diets. The estimated average requirement (EAR) meets the needs of half a healthy group. The recommended dietary allowance (RDA) covers nearly all healthy people; it is usually EAR plus two standard deviations of requirement. The adequate intake (AI) is a judged sufficient intake used when an EAR cannot be set. The tolerable upper intake level (UL) is the highest usual intake unlikely to cause harm. Values come from balance studies, deficiency and toxicity evidence, and uncertainty factors.

Hypothetical example: EAR = 40 mg/day and standard deviation = 10 mg/day, so RDA = 40 + (2 × 10) = 60 mg/day. The UL is a ceiling, not a target.

sections.heading: National terms
sections.text:
Countries use different names. The United States and Canada use Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs), with EAR, RDA, AI and UL. The United Kingdom uses Dietary Reference Values (DRVs): EAR, reference nutrient intake (RNI), lower reference nutrient intake (LRNI) and safe intake. The European Union uses average requirement (AR), population reference intake (PRI), AI and UL. WHO and FAO publish recommended nutrient intakes. Numbers differ by population and year; check national or WHO guidance.

Use the EAR for group inadequacy, the RDA or AI for individuals, and the UL to flag excess.

sections.heading: Guidelines and labels
sections.text:
Food-based dietary guidelines (FBDGs) translate nutrient needs into practical food patterns. They describe local foods, meals and habits for a country or region. They promote variety, fruits and vegetables, suitable staples, and limited salt, sugar and unhealthy fats. FBDGs are public health advice, not a clinical prescription.

Front-of-pack (FOP) labelling summarises a packaged food’s nutrient profile. Examples include UK traffic-light labels, Nutri-Score in France and some European countries, and Health Star Rating in Australia and New Zealand. FOP labels are communication tools; they do not replace the nutrition panel or a nutrient standard.

Nutrient standards are numerical benchmarks; FBDGs and FOP labels are aids. A diet can meet an RDA yet lack variety, so use both.

keyPoints: EAR is the median requirement; RDA is usually EAR + 2 standard deviations.
AI is used when an EAR cannot be set; UL is the highest usual intake unlikely to cause harm.
Country terms differ: DRIs in the US and Canada, DRVs and RNI in the UK, AR and PRI in the EU.
Use the EAR for group inadequacy, the RDA or AI for individuals, and the UL to flag excess.
FBDGs translate nutrient needs into local food patterns and are public health advice, not clinical prescriptions.
Front-of-pack labels summarise nutrient profile but do not replace nutrient standards or the nutrition panel.

en.title: Maternal and infant nutrition
en.short: Pregnancy and lactation needs, micronutrients, breastfeeding, WHO Code, complementary feeding and growth monitoring.

sections.heading: Pregnancy and lactation
sections.text: Pregnancy raises needs for energy, protein and micronutrients. Energy need rises mainly in later pregnancy; lactation also needs extra energy and fluid. Requirements vary by activity and country, so use current national or WHO guidance. Weight gain is checked against a range set by pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI, weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared). Too little gain risks poor fetal growth; too much raises complications. Folate before conception and early in pregnancy helps prevent neural tube defects. Iron supports the fetus and maternal blood; supplements follow national policy where anaemia is common. Iodine is needed for thyroid hormones and brain development; iodised salt helps. Doses vary by country.

sections.heading: Breastfeeding and Code
sections.text: Breast milk provides energy, antibodies and protective factors. Colostrum, the first thick milk, is rich in immune factors. WHO advises exclusive breastfeeding for about six months, then continued breastfeeding with complementary foods to two years or beyond. The WHO International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes controls marketing of breast-milk substitutes, bottles and teats. It does not ban products; it protects informed feeding. Health workers should support breastfeeding and not promote substitutes.

sections.heading: Complementary feeding
sections.text: From about six months, breast milk alone no longer meets needs. Complementary feeding means giving safe, adequate and responsive foods while breastfeeding continues. Start soft, nutrient-dense foods; increase variety and texture with age. Include iron-rich foods. National programmes may advise fortified foods or supplements. Growth monitoring means plotting weight, length and head circumference on growth charts, such as WHO Child Growth Standards for under-fives. The trend matters more than one point; falling across lines needs assessment.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Amina, 24, books at 12 weeks. Her weight is 58 kg; at 36 weeks it is 69 kg. The recorded gain is 69 − 58 = 11 kg. The nurse compares it with the range for Amina’s pre-pregnancy BMI in current guidance, then counsels on diet, folate, iron, iodine and breastfeeding. No single number decides care.

keyPoints: Pregnancy and lactation increase energy, protein and micronutrient needs; use current national or WHO guidance.
Weight gain should be monitored against the range for pre-pregnancy BMI.
Folate before conception and early pregnancy prevents neural tube defects; iron and iodine needs are met through diet and national supplementation or fortification policy.
Exclusive breastfeeding for about six months, with continued breastfeeding to two years or beyond, is WHO advice.
The WHO International Code regulates marketing of breast-milk substitutes; it does not ban them.
Complementary feeding starts about six months; growth monitoring uses plotted trends on WHO growth standards.

en.title: Child and adolescent nutrition
en.short: Growth, nutrient needs, school feeding, undernutrition, obesity, adolescent pregnancy, sport and family education.

sections.heading: Growth and needs
sections.text: Growth is fastest in infancy and at puberty. From preschool to adolescence, energy and protein needs per kilogram fall, but total needs rise. Puberty raises iron, calcium and zinc needs. Growth is checked against WHO Child Growth Standards for under 5 years and WHO Growth Reference for 5 to 19 years. Stunting is low height for age, a sign of long-term undernutrition. Wasting is low weight for height, a sign of recent severe undernutrition. Obesity is excess body fat, screened with body mass index for age (weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared).

sections.heading: School feeding and double burden
sections.text: School feeding provides meals or snacks in school. Well-designed programmes set nutrition standards, include fruit, vegetables, legumes and fortified foods, and can support attendance and diet quality. They should not replace family meals. The double burden means undernutrition and obesity can coexist in one child or community. A stunted child may become obese later. Children with obesity need family-based support and healthy routines, not restrictive dieting. Severe undernutrition needs referral under national guidance.

sections.heading: Adolescent pregnancy and sport
sections.text: Adolescent pregnancy adds nutrient needs to ongoing growth. Iron, folate, calcium and energy needs rise. Care should follow current WHO and national antenatal guidance, with early booking and supplements as prescribed. Adolescent athletes need enough energy and carbohydrate for training, plus iron and calcium. Low energy availability can cause relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S), with poor growth, menstrual problems and injury. Supplements are not a substitute for food.

sections.heading: Education for families
sections.text: Nutrition education for children and families should be practical and respectful of culture and income. Teach food groups, label reading, safe cooking and portion sizes. Involve caregivers and the whole school food environment. Avoid blame and restrictive language. Case: a school in Kaduna starts a breakfast club with pap, milk and fruit, and a parent workshop on packed lunches. Attendance rises and children bring water instead of sweet drinks. The school reviews the plan each term with families.

keyPoints: Growth is fastest in infancy and puberty; use WHO growth standards for under 5 years and WHO reference for 5 to 19 years.
Stunting reflects long-term undernutrition and wasting reflects recent severe undernutrition.
School feeding can improve diet quality and attendance when it meets nutrition standards and does not replace family meals.
The double burden means undernutrition and obesity can coexist in the same child or community.
Adolescent pregnancy raises iron, folate, calcium and energy needs; follow current WHO and national antenatal guidance.
Nutrition education works best when it involves families and the whole school food environment.

en.title: Adult and older adult nutrition
en.short: Nutrient needs, body changes, oral health, medicines and malnutrition in ageing adults.

sections.heading: Needs in adulthood
sections.text: Adulthood is long, so needs differ between a young worker and a frail person over 70. Energy needs generally fall with age as lean mass and activity decrease. Protein, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12 need attention, but requirements vary by country and clinical state. National dietary guidelines and WHO guidance give current values. Varied meals in enough quantity usually meet most needs; restrictive diets, poor dentition or illness raise risk.

sections.heading: Body composition
sections.text: Ageing changes body composition. Muscle mass and strength decline; when marked, this is sarcopenia. It reduces mobility and increases falls. Bone mass is lost after midlife, faster in women after menopause, raising osteoporosis and fracture risk. Weight may stay stable while fat rises and muscle falls, so body mass index can hide risk. Resistance exercise and adequate protein and vitamin D help; follow local guidance.

sections.heading: Oral health and medicines
sections.text: Oral health affects nutrition. Missing teeth, badly fitting dentures, dry mouth and gum disease make chewing painful, so people choose soft, less nutritious foods and may eat less protein and fewer nutrients. Swallowing difficulty, called dysphagia, raises choking and aspiration (food entering the airway) risk. It needs assessment by a trained clinician; texture-modified food or thickened fluids only under that advice. Many older adults take several medicines, called polypharmacy. Medicines can cause dry mouth, nausea, constipation or poor appetite, and some interact with food. Review medicines with a pharmacist or prescriber.

sections.heading: Malnutrition and care
sections.text: Malnutrition in older people is common and often missed. It means poor intake or absorption leading to loss of weight and muscle, not simply being thin. Screen with a validated tool such as the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), then assess further. Community support includes shopping help, meals, food fortification and social eating. In care homes, observe intake, respect preferences and give help at meals. Case: an 82-year-old widow living alone eats only tea and bread because her dentures hurt. Dental review, softer protein foods and a shared lunch improve intake. Guidelines change, so check current national or WHO advice.

keyPoints: Energy needs often fall with age as lean mass and activity decrease, but protein, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12 remain important.
Sarcopenia is age-related loss of muscle mass and strength, and it raises falls and disability.
Bone loss after midlife, especially after menopause, increases osteoporosis, meaning thin and fragile bone, and fracture risk.
Poor oral health and dysphagia can reduce intake and raise the risk of aspiration, food entering the airway; assess before changing food texture.
Polypharmacy can cause dry mouth, nausea, constipation or poor appetite, so review medicines regularly.
Screen older people for malnutrition and support meals, food fortification and social eating in community and care settings, following current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Undernutrition and micronutrient deficiencies
en.short: Stunting, wasting, underweight and micronutrient deficiencies: causes, assessment, treatment principles and control.

sections.heading: Definitions and causes
sections.text:
Undernutrition means insufficient energy, protein or micronutrients for needs. Stunting is low height-for-age, reflecting long-term undernutrition and infection. Wasting is low weight-for-height, reflecting recent acute loss. Severe acute malnutrition is identified by very low weight-for-height, low mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) or nutritional oedema (swelling due to malnutrition). Underweight is low weight-for-age. Micronutrient deficiencies are shortages of vitamins or minerals, such as iron, vitamin A, iodine and zinc.

Causes are immediate, underlying and basic. Immediate causes are inadequate diet and disease. Underlying causes include food insecurity, poor feeding and care, unsafe water and weak health services. Basic causes include poverty and inequality. Repeated diarrhoea with a monotonous diet can lead to wasting and then stunting.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.text: Assessment uses anthropometry plotted on growth standards, MUAC, oedema check, dietary and illness history, and clinical signs. Laboratory tests help where available. Classify acute malnutrition as severe or moderate using current WHO or national criteria, alongside a full clinical assessment. Look for danger signs and complications.

sections.heading: Treatment principles
sections.text:
Management follows current WHO and national protocols. Severe acute malnutrition with complications or poor appetite needs inpatient care: treat infection and dehydration, correct electrolytes, give therapeutic food in staged amounts, and monitor. Uncomplicated cases can often be treated as outpatients with ready-to-use therapeutic food and follow-up. Moderate acute malnutrition needs supplementary feeding, counselling and treatment of underlying illness.

Case: Amina, 18 months, has oedema and low MUAC. She is admitted, treated for infection, and fed by the local severe malnutrition protocol. After stabilisation she receives counselling and follow-up.

sections.heading: Control strategies
sections.text: Control combines supplementation, fortification and dietary diversification. Vitamin A, iron and folic acid supplements, and multiple micronutrient powders are used in defined groups by national policy. Fortification adds nutrients to staples such as flour, oil or salt; iodised salt is a common example. Dietary diversification supports varied, nutrient-rich diets through nutrition education, home gardens and improved food access. Breastfeeding promotion, infection control and food security are also essential. Check current WHO and national guidance.

keyPoints: Stunting is low height-for-age; wasting is low weight-for-height; underweight is low weight-for-age.
Severe acute malnutrition is identified by very low weight-for-height, low MUAC or nutritional oedema.
Causes operate at immediate, underlying and basic levels, including diet, disease, food insecurity and poverty.
Classify acute malnutrition as severe or moderate using current WHO or national criteria, alongside a full assessment.
Severe acute malnutrition with complications needs inpatient protocol care; uncomplicated cases may be treated as outpatients with ready-to-use therapeutic food.
Control combines supplementation, fortification, dietary diversification and attention to food security and infection.

en.title: Obesity and weight management
en.short: Measuring obesity, its causes and stigma, and the principles of weight management.

sections.heading: Definitions and measurement
sections.text:
Body mass index (BMI) is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared: BMI = kg ÷ m². For 90 kg and 1.70 m: 1.70 × 1.70 = 2.89, and 90 ÷ 2.89 = 31.1 kg/m². WHO bands: under 18.5 underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 normal, 25 to 29.9 overweight, 30 or more obesity. BMI screens; it cannot separate fat from muscle, and some countries use lower cut-offs for Asian populations.

Waist circumference measures central fat and adds risk information. Thresholds differ by sex and population; commonly cited Europid values are above 94 cm in men and 80 cm in women for increased risk, and above 102 cm and 88 cm for substantially increased risk.

sections.heading: Causes, consequences and stigma
sections.text:
Obesity comes from energy intake above expenditure over time, shaped by genetics, sleep, medicines, endocrine disease and environments that make energy-dense food cheap and activity easy to avoid. Consequences include type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, some cancers, sleep apnoea, osteoarthritis and reduced fertility.

Weight stigma is blaming or shaming people with obesity. It harms mental health, discourages care and does not motivate. Use person-first language: a person with obesity.

sections.heading: Principles of weight management
sections.text:
Weight management aims at a sustained energy deficit. Losing 5 to 10 per cent of body weight already improves blood pressure, glucose and lipids. No single diet is best; the useful pattern is one the person can keep, usually with more vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains and fewer sugary drinks and energy-dense snacks.

Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus muscle strengthening; activity mainly helps maintenance. Behaviour change uses self-monitoring, realistic goals, planning for lapses and social support.

sections.heading: Specialist treatment
sections.text: Specialist referral is considered when BMI is high with related disease, when lifestyle change has not worked, or when an eating disorder or endocrine cause is suspected. Medicines and bariatric (weight-loss) surgery are clinical decisions; criteria vary by country, so check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: BMI = weight in kg ÷ height in m²; 90 kg at 1.70 m gives 31.1 kg/m².
WHO bands: 18.5 to 24.9 normal, 25 to 29.9 overweight, 30 or more obesity.
Waist circumference shows central fat and adds risk beyond BMI.
Obesity has many causes; stigma harms and does not motivate.
A 5 to 10 per cent weight loss already improves metabolic health.
Medicines and surgery are clinical decisions with criteria that vary by country.

en.title: Nutrition therapy in diabetes
en.short: Types, goals, carbohydrate, fibre, GI, weight, hypoglycaemia, sick days and cultural adaptation.

sections.heading: Types and goals
sections.text: Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders with high blood glucose. Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells. Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency. Gestational diabetes first appears in pregnancy, and other specific types have known causes such as pancreatic disease. Nutrition therapy, also called medical nutrition therapy, is part of treatment for all types. Its goals are to support safe glucose levels, blood pressure and lipids, prevent complications, meet nutritional needs and protect quality of life. Targets are individualised; check current national and WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Carbohydrate and meals
sections.text: Carbohydrate amount matters, especially with insulin. Consistency helps. Quality also matters: choose whole grains, legumes, vegetables and fruit. Fibre slows absorption and improves control; many guidelines suggest about 25 to 30 g daily for adults, but needs vary. Glycaemic index ranks foods by the glucose rise they cause. Low glycaemic index foods are useful, but portion size still matters. Meal patterns should be regular and suit culture, work and insulin. For example, if a meal contains 45 g carbohydrate and the plan uses 15 g portions, that meal is three portions.

sections.heading: Weight, lows and culture
sections.text: Overweight in type 2 diabetes: modest, sustained weight loss improves glucose. Support realistic changes. Hypoglycaemia is low blood glucose, often below 3.9 mmol/L. Teach symptoms and local fast-carbohydrate treatment, then recheck. On sick days, monitor glucose more often, drink fluids, continue insulin unless advised otherwise, and seek help for vomiting or high readings. Adapt advice to local staples, income, religion and family. Use local foods and examples, and involve family. Refer to current national and WHO guidance rather than fixed protocols. People need individual advice from their care team.

keyPoints: Type 1, type 2 and gestational diabetes all need individualised nutrition therapy.
Carbohydrate amount and quality both matter; fibre and low-GI foods help.
Meal patterns should be regular and culturally suitable.
Modest sustained weight loss improves type 2 diabetes control.
Treat hypoglycaemia with fast carbohydrate and recheck, following local guidance.
On sick days, monitor glucose, keep fluids and do not stop insulin without advice.

en.title: Nutrition in cardiovascular disease
en.short: Dietary fats, sodium, fibre, DASH and Mediterranean patterns, and counselling for hypertension and dyslipidaemia.

sections.heading: Fats and cholesterol
sections.text: Fat type matters more than total fat. Saturated fat raises low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol; trans fat raises LDL and lowers high-density lipoprotein (HDL). Replace them with unsaturated fats from nuts, seeds, oily fish and oils. Dietary cholesterol matters less for most people. The World Health Organization (WHO) suggests total fat under 30% of energy, saturated fat under 10% and trans fat under 1%; national targets differ, so check guidance. Example: on a 2,000 kcal diet, 30% fat is 600 kcal. Fat gives 9 kcal/g, so 600 ÷ 9 = 66.7 g fat; 10% saturated fat is 200 ÷ 9 = 22.2 g.

sections.heading: Sodium and blood pressure
sections.text: High sodium intake raises blood pressure in many people. WHO recommends less than 2 g sodium a day for adults, about 5 g salt, but national targets vary. Most sodium comes from processed foods and salt added during cooking, not just the salt shaker at the table. Reducing sodium lowers blood pressure, especially in older adults and people with hypertension (high blood pressure). Increasing potassium-rich fruit and vegetables helps, but people with kidney disease need medical advice before increasing potassium.

sections.heading: Fibre and dietary patterns
sections.text: Dietary fibre from whole grains, legumes, fruit and vegetables lowers LDL cholesterol and may reduce cardiovascular risk. Soluble fibre, such as oats and beans, binds bile acids. Many guidelines suggest about 25 to 30 g fibre a day for adults, but targets vary. The Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) pattern emphasises fruit, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy, legumes and nuts, and limits salt, sweets and saturated fat. The Mediterranean pattern emphasises plant foods, olive oil, fish and little processed meat. Both patterns are associated with lower cardiovascular risk in observational studies and trials.

sections.heading: Nutrition counselling
sections.text: Nutrition counselling for hypertension and dyslipidaemia (abnormal blood lipids) starts with assessment of usual diet, weight, blood pressure and lipid results. Set one or two specific goals, such as replacing processed snacks with fruit or using less stock cube. Use motivational interviewing and involve the family. Review progress and refer for medication decisions. Guidelines change, so follow current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Saturated and trans fats raise LDL cholesterol; replace them with unsaturated fats.
WHO suggests total fat under 30% of energy, saturated fat under 10% and trans fat under 1%; national targets vary.
Fat grams = fat kilocalories ÷ 9; on a 2,000 kcal diet, 30% fat is 600 ÷ 9 = 66.7 g.
WHO recommends less than 2 g sodium a day for adults, about 5 g salt; most sodium comes from processed foods and salt added during cooking.
DASH and Mediterranean patterns emphasise plant foods and are linked to lower cardiovascular risk.
Counselling should set small goals and follow current national or WHO guidance; it is not a substitute for medical care.

en.title: Nutrition in kidney disease
en.short: Diet in chronic kidney disease: staging, protein, sodium, potassium, phosphate, fluid and dialysis.

sections.heading: Staging CKD
sections.text: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) means kidney damage or reduced kidney function lasting more than three months. Staging uses two main measures, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR, in mL/min/1.73 m²) and albuminuria, together with the underlying cause. Albuminuria is measured as the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) in mg/g (mg/mmol in some countries). eGFR categories run from G1 (90 or above, with damage) through G2 (60 to 89), G3a (45 to 59), G3b (30 to 44), G4 (15 to 29) to G5 (below 15, kidney failure). Albuminuria runs from A1 (below 30) to A2 (30 to 300) to A3 (above 300). Higher stage and albuminuria mean higher risk. Diet needs change with stage, dialysis, laboratory results and other illnesses.

sections.heading: Diet considerations
sections.text: Diet therapy is individual. In non-dialysis CKD, a modest protein restriction may reduce nitrogen waste, while enough energy prevents the body using protein for fuel. Dialysis removes amino acids and protein, so needs often rise. Sodium restriction means less salt and fewer processed foods; it helps blood pressure and fluid control. Potassium is not restricted for everyone: decide from serum potassium, medicines, urine output and dialysis. Phosphate control limits phosphate additives in processed foods and may need prescribed binders. Fluid is restricted only for fluid overload or low urine output, not routinely.

sections.heading: Dialysis and conservative care
sections.text: Haemodialysis is intermittent; peritoneal dialysis is continuous and can cause protein loss. Both need regular review of weight, blood pressure, fluid, potassium, phosphate and albumin. Conservative kidney management is active care without dialysis: treat symptoms, adjust diet to what the person eats and tolerates, and plan support. It is a valid choice, not a failure of care.

sections.heading: Monitoring and counselling
sections.text: The dietitian assesses intake, weight, appetite, laboratory results and medicines, then sets practical targets and reviews them. Counselling covers food labels, portion sizes, cooking, fluids and avoiding unproven herbal products. Example: a 60 kg patient with a dietitian-set protein target of 0.8 g/kg needs 60 × 0.8 = 48 g protein daily. This is an illustration, not a universal prescription; current national or KDIGO guidance and the renal team decide.

keyPoints: CKD is staged by eGFR G1 to G5, albuminuria A1 to A3 and the underlying cause.
Diet changes depend on stage, dialysis, laboratory results and other illnesses.
Protein restriction may be used before dialysis; dialysis often increases protein needs.
Sodium restriction helps blood pressure and fluid control; potassium and fluid limits are not automatic.
Phosphate control focuses on additives and prescribed binders.
The dietitian monitors and counsels; protein target = body weight × g/kg.

en.title: Nutrition in gastrointestinal, liver and allergic disease
en.short: Malabsorption, coeliac disease, IBD, IBS, liver disease, food allergy and elimination diets.

sections.heading: Malabsorption and coeliac
sections.text: Malabsorption means poor absorption of nutrients from the gut. It causes diarrhoea, weight loss, anaemia and deficiencies. Causes include coeliac disease, Crohn’s disease, gut infection and pancreatic disease. Coeliac disease is an immune reaction to gluten in wheat, barley and rye. It damages small bowel villi and reduces absorption. Symptoms vary; some people have none. Diagnosis uses blood tests and biopsy while the person still eats gluten. Do not start a gluten-free diet before testing. Treatment is a lifelong strict gluten-free diet with dietitian support and deficiency checks.

sections.heading: IBD and IBS
sections.text: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) includes Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis: chronic immune inflammation of the gut. Nutrition care treats malnutrition and deficiencies such as iron, vitamin B12 and vitamin D. In some children with Crohn’s disease, exclusive enteral nutrition can induce remission; practice varies by country. Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional disorder with gut pain and changed bowel habit but no inflammation. Diet eases symptoms but does not cure. A low FODMAP (fermentable carbohydrate) diet is short-term, with a trained dietitian, then reintroduction.

sections.heading: Liver and allergy
sections.text: Liver disease, especially cirrhosis, causes poor appetite, muscle wasting and deficiencies. Do not routinely restrict protein; current guidance advises adequate protein even in hepatic encephalopathy, with specialist input. Small frequent meals and a late evening snack may help. Avoid alcohol. Food allergy is an immune reaction, often IgE-mediated and sometimes severe (anaphylaxis). Food intolerance is non-immune, such as lactose intolerance. Elimination diets risk nutrient deficiencies, poor growth in children and food aversion. Remove only confirmed allergens, with dietitian follow-up.

sections.heading: Referral and case
sections.text: Refer suspected coeliac disease, IBD, liver disease or food allergy to a dietitian and specialist. Refer before starting an elimination diet. Seek urgent care for severe allergic reactions. Case: Amina, a 24-year-old student in Nigeria, had chronic diarrhoea and anaemia. Blood tests and biopsy confirmed coeliac disease. A dietitian started a gluten-free diet and checked iron and vitamins. Her symptoms improved. Guidelines differ; check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Malabsorption causes diarrhoea, weight loss, anaemia and deficiencies; causes include coeliac disease, IBD, infection and pancreatic disease.
Coeliac disease is an immune reaction to gluten; diagnosis needs testing while gluten is still eaten, and treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet.
In IBD, treat malnutrition and deficiencies; IBS is functional and diet eases symptoms but does not cure.
In liver disease, do not restrict protein, even in hepatic encephalopathy; current guidance advises adequate protein with specialist care.
Food allergy is immune and can be severe; food intolerance is non-immune; elimination diets risk deficiencies and poor growth.
Refer to a dietitian and specialist for suspected coeliac disease, IBD, liver disease, allergy, and before elimination diets.

en.title: Nutrition in cancer, HIV and palliative care
en.short: Cancer cachexia, HIV and TB nutrition, food safety, and ethical palliative feeding and hydration.

sections.heading: Cancer cachexia
sections.text:
Cancer cachexia is a multifactorial syndrome of involuntary weight loss, muscle wasting and anorexia (loss of appetite) caused by illness, not simply by low intake. Nutrition support means counselling, food fortification, oral supplements, or tube feeding into the gut (enteral) or vein (parenteral) to meet needs.

Support cannot usually reverse cachexia. Aim for early screening, symptom control and small, frequent high energy and protein meals. Tube or intravenous feeding is considered only when it fits the person’s goals; aggressive feeding near death can cause distress.

sections.heading: HIV and TB
sections.text:
HIV infection and tuberculosis (TB) increase undernutrition risk. HIV raises energy needs and can cause mouth problems, diarrhoea and poor appetite. TB causes weight loss and higher energy and protein needs. Assess weight, appetite, food access and symptoms. Aim for adequate energy, protein and micronutrients from food; treat confirmed deficiencies. Avoid large micronutrient doses without guidance because some interact with treatment.

Antiretroviral therapy and TB treatment are central; nutrition supports adherence and recovery. WHO and national guidelines give current advice.

sections.heading: Food safety
sections.text: People with weakened immunity from advanced HIV, cancer treatment or transplant need safe food. Cook meat, eggs and fish thoroughly; avoid raw or unpasteurised foods; wash fruit and vegetables with safe water; keep raw and cooked foods separate; refrigerate promptly; wash hands. Strict low-microbe diets are not uniformly recommended; follow local advice.

sections.heading: Palliative care and ethics
sections.text:
Palliative care aims at comfort and quality of life. Food and drink are social and emotional, not only calories. Offer small portions, favourite foods and mouth care. Artificial hydration (fluids by tube or vein) may relieve thirst but can cause fluid overload, breathlessness or secretions; evidence does not show it always improves comfort.

Decisions respect autonomy (the person’s wishes), beneficence (do good), nonmaleficence (avoid harm) and justice (fairness). Assess capacity, involve family, record the person’s future wishes. National law applies. Case: man with advanced cancer refuses food. Do not force feeding; offer mouth care and tastes, and discuss goals with him.

keyPoints: Cancer cachexia is a metabolic syndrome; nutrition support alone rarely reverses it.
In HIV and TB, treat the infection and support adequate energy, protein and micronutrients; avoid unsupervised high-dose supplements.
Food safety during immunosuppression means thorough cooking, safe water, separation of raw and cooked foods and avoiding unpasteurised products.
Artificial hydration may relieve thirst but can worsen fluid overload and breathlessness; assess comfort individually.
Ethical feeding respects autonomy, capacity, beneficence and nonmaleficence, and local law and policy apply.
Palliative nutrition aims at comfort and quality of life, not forced intake.

en.title: Clinical nutrition support
en.short: Hospital screening, refeeding risk, enteral and parenteral feeding, monitoring and team care.

sections.heading: Screening and assessment
sections.text: Nutrition screening is a quick check to find patients who are malnourished or at risk. It uses recent weight loss, low body mass index, reduced intake and disease severity. A positive screen leads to fuller assessment by a dietitian or trained clinician. Assessment covers weight history, intake, symptoms, physical signs, biochemistry and social factors. In hospital, record weight and height when possible, watch for fluid retention, and repeat screening. Use a validated tool approved locally; tools and cut-offs vary by country and setting.

sections.heading: Refeeding syndrome
sections.text: Refeeding syndrome is a shift in chemistry when nutrition is restarted in a malnourished person. Insulin release drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, so blood levels fall. This can cause weakness, heart rhythm problems and organ failure. Risk is higher after prolonged low intake, major weight loss or severe illness. Consider thiamine before feeding as local guidance advises, start nutrition cautiously and monitor electrolytes closely. Prevention matters more than treatment.

sections.heading: Enteral and parenteral
sections.text: Enteral nutrition delivers nutrients into the gut through a tube, such as nasogastric or gastrostomy. It is preferred when the gut works: it is physiological, cheaper and carries fewer serious infections. Parenteral nutrition gives nutrients into a vein, bypassing the gut. It is used when the gut cannot be used safely or adequately. Both need a clear indication, suitable formula, aseptic care and review. Enteral feeding can cause aspiration, diarrhoea or tube problems. Parenteral feeding can cause line infection, blood clots and metabolic disturbances.

sections.heading: Monitoring and team
sections.text: Monitor intake, weight, fluid balance, electrolytes, glucose and tolerance. Check tube position and line sites. A multidisciplinary team improves care: doctors diagnose and treat, dietitians assess and plan, nurses monitor and deliver, pharmacists review medicines, and speech therapists advise on swallowing safety. For example, Amina, a 19-year-old student with severe weight loss after surgery, is screened, assessed, fed cautiously and reviewed daily. Follow local protocols and current WHO guidance, which change.

keyPoints: Nutrition screening identifies risk; positive screens need fuller assessment.
Refeeding syndrome causes low phosphate, potassium and magnesium after nutrition restarts.
Start feeding cautiously in at-risk patients and monitor electrolytes closely.
Enteral nutrition is preferred when the gut works; parenteral nutrition bypasses the gut.
Monitor intake, weight, fluids, electrolytes, glucose, tube position and line sites.
The multidisciplinary team includes doctors, dietitians, nurses, pharmacists and speech therapists.

en.title: Public health nutrition
en.short: Population nutrition problems, double burden, food security, policy, fortification and evaluation.

sections.heading: Population problems
sections.text:
Public health nutrition works at population level. It asks how many people are affected, who is affected and why, then designs actions for communities rather than individual patients. Common problems include stunting, wasting, micronutrient deficiencies, overweight and diet-related disease.

The double burden of malnutrition is the coexistence of undernutrition and overnutrition in the same country, community, household or person. It reflects changing diets, activity and food systems, often called the nutrition transition.

sections.heading: Food security and environments
sections.text:
Food security is commonly defined by FAO as when all people, at all times, have physical, social and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food. Its pillars are availability, access, utilisation and stability.

The food environment is the physical, economic, policy and socio-cultural setting that shapes what people can buy and eat. A neighbourhood with cheap processed snacks but few affordable fresh foods illustrates a poor food environment. Food policy can change it through taxes, subsidies, labelling, marketing rules, school food standards and trade rules.

sections.heading: Policy and programmes
sections.text:
Fortification adds vitamins or minerals to widely eaten staples, such as iodised salt or fortified flour. It works when the food is consumed regularly, the level is safe, and quality is monitored.

Supplementation gives concentrated micronutrients to groups at higher risk, such as young children or pregnant women; national and WHO guidance set target groups and schedules. Both need supply, coverage, adherence and safety monitoring. Policy choices involve trade-offs, so check current national guidance.

sections.heading: Evaluating interventions
sections.text:
Evaluation asks whether a programme was implemented as planned, reached the intended group, changed outcomes and offered good value. Process indicators include coverage; outcome indicators include deficiency or growth measures.

For example, a fictional district plans to reach 10,000 households. Monitoring finds 7,500 received fortified flour, so coverage is 7,500 ÷ 10,000 × 100 = 75%. If 6,000 used it regularly, effective coverage is 6,000 ÷ 10,000 × 100 = 60%. Before-after comparisons can mislead because other things change, so controlled designs are stronger when feasible.

keyPoints: Public health nutrition addresses population-level problems and their determinants, not only individual care.
The double burden is undernutrition and overnutrition coexisting in a country, community, household or person.
Food security has four pillars: availability, access, utilisation and stability.
Food environments and food policy shape what people can buy and eat.
Fortification and supplementation need targeting, quality control, coverage and safety monitoring.
Evaluate process, coverage, outcomes and cost; coverage = people reached ÷ target population × 100.

en.title: Nutrition education and counselling
en.short: Behaviour change, counselling, health literacy and evaluating nutrition education materials.

sections.heading: Behaviour change theories
sections.text:
Nutrition education supports people to make their own food choices; facts rarely change behaviour. Behaviour change theories help plan support.

The Stages of Change model describes readiness: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance. Social Cognitive Theory stresses self-efficacy, confidence to act, and home, work and community influences. The Health Belief Model weighs perceived risk, severity, benefits and barriers. The Theory of Planned Behaviour links attitudes, social norms and perceived control to intention. Use theory to shape questions; do not label people.

sections.heading: Client-centred counselling
sections.text:
Counselling is a structured conversation to help a person decide and act. Client-centred practice means the client sets the agenda. Motivational interviewing (MI) is a collaborative, goal-oriented style that draws out the person’s own reasons for change.

Core skills are open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries (OARS). Avoid arguing or telling the person what to do; this can increase resistance. MI explores ambivalence, feeling two ways about change. It is not a substitute for clinical care; follow current national or WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Health literacy and culture
sections.text:
Health literacy is the ability to find, understand, judge and use health information. It is not a sign of intelligence. Use plain words, short sentences, pictures and teach-back: ask the person to explain the plan in their own words.

Cultural sensitivity means respecting food beliefs, language, gender roles and money limits. Ask about staple foods and who shops and cooks. A counsellor in Ibadan asks market women which green leafy vegetables and dried fish are affordable and acceptable, rather than naming only costly foods.

sections.heading: Materials and communication
sections.text:
To develop materials, assess needs and set clear objectives. Write in the local language, use familiar foods and pictures, and pretest with a small group. Evaluation has three levels: process (was it delivered and used?), impact (knowledge, confidence, intention) and outcome (behaviour or nutritional status).

For groups, facilitate discussion and practical demonstrations rather than lecture. For individuals, listen, reflect and agree one small next step. Record what was agreed and refer when needs exceed your role.

keyPoints: Nutrition education supports informed choice; knowledge alone rarely changes behaviour.
Behaviour change theories guide planning and questioning, not the labelling of people.
Motivational interviewing is client-centred and uses OARS; avoid arguing and respect autonomy.
Health literacy and cultural sensitivity shape plain-language, teach-back and food-based messages.
Pretest materials and evaluate at process, impact and outcome levels.
Refer beyond your role and follow current national or WHO guidance for clinical decisions.

en.title: Food service systems and management
en.short: Menu planning, procurement, production, distribution, HACCP, cost control and staffing in food service.

sections.heading: Menu planning and procurement
sections.text: Menu planning turns nutrition requirements and patient needs into meals. A menu cycle is a set of menus repeated over days. Plan for nutritional adequacy, therapeutic diets, texture, culture, season, equipment, labour and cost. Procurement is buying food and supplies. Use written specifications for quality, quantity and delivery, compare suppliers, and check goods on receipt. Store foods correctly, rotate stock using first in, first out, and keep records.

sections.heading: Production, distribution and safety
sections.text: Production uses standard recipes and portion control so meals are consistent. Distribution may be bulk, plated or tray service; keep hot food hot and cold food cold, and record temperatures. HACCP means Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point. It is a preventive system with seven principles: identify hazards, find critical control points, set limits, monitor them, act when limits are missed, verify the system and keep records. A critical control point is a step where control is essential to prevent or reduce a food safety hazard. For example, cooking poultry to a safe internal temperature is a critical control point. Follow current national food safety law and Codex guidance.

sections.heading: Quality, cost and staffing
sections.text: Quality control checks meals against agreed standards: appearance, taste, nutrition, safety and patient satisfaction. Cost control compares budget with actual spending. Food cost percentage is food cost divided by food sales, multiplied by 100. If food cost is 240,000 and sales are 600,000, the percentage is 240,000 ÷ 600,000 × 100 = 40%. Staffing needs clear roles, training, supervision and workload planning. Food service staff need food hygiene training; dietitians and managers need leadership and communication skills.

sections.heading: Dietitian’s role
sections.text: The dietitian links nutrition care with food service. In hospital, the dietitian prescribes therapeutic diets, reviews menus, trains catering staff and monitors intake. In community services, the dietitian advises on meals for schools, care homes and feeding programmes. Work with caterers, nurses and managers, and check current national guidance because standards change.

keyPoints: Menu planning must meet nutrition, therapeutic, cultural, equipment and cost needs.
Procurement uses specifications, supplier checks, correct storage and stock rotation.
HACCP is a preventive food safety system with seven principles and records.
Food cost percentage = food cost ÷ food sales × 100.
Staff need clear roles, hygiene training, supervision and workload planning.
The dietitian links therapeutic diets and community nutrition with catering practice, following current national guidance.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and law in dietetics
en.short: Scope, ethics, consent, confidentiality, teamwork, regulation and legal issues in dietetic practice.

sections.heading: Scope and standards
sections.text: Scope of practice is the range of tasks a dietitian is trained, competent and permitted to do. Law, regulators, employers and personal competence shape it.
