Dietitians assess nutritional status, plan and monitor nutrition therapy, educate, and work in food service or public health. The title nutritionist and its scope vary: some countries protect dietitian but not nutritionist; others regulate both or neither. Codes of ethics state duties such as competence, honesty, dignity, confidentiality and avoiding harm. They guide judgement but do not replace the law.

sections.heading: Ethics and consent
sections.text: Informed consent means the person understands the purpose, benefits, risks and alternatives, and agrees freely. Consent can be withdrawn. Confidentiality means keeping personal health information private. Share it only with consent or when law or serious risk justifies it, and share the minimum necessary. Case: Chidi, a dietitian in Lagos, is asked by a patient’s employer for her diet record. Chidi explains confidentiality, obtains the patient’s written consent, and sends only the needed information. A conflict of interest is a financial or personal interest that may bias judgement. Declare and manage it, such as by refusing a gift that could influence advice.

sections.heading: Teamwork and regulation
sections.text: Dietitians work in teams with doctors, nurses, pharmacists, speech therapists and community workers. Good teamwork needs clear roles, respectful communication, referral when a task is outside your competence, and shared records. Regulation and licensure differ by country. Licensure is legal permission to practise a protected title or role. Some have a statutory council; others rely on voluntary registration. Check the current national regulator, registration requirements and scope rules before you practise. Regulation protects the public through entry standards, conduct rules and complaints processes.

sections.heading: Legal issues
sections.text: Legal issues include negligence, documentation, privacy, consent, advertising and misleading claims. Negligence requires a duty of care, a breach, harm and a causal link. Keep records factual, dated and secure. Do not make false therapeutic claims. Laws and reporting duties vary; follow employer policy and current national law.

keyPoints: Scope of practice is shaped by law, regulators, employers and your own competence.
Informed consent must be voluntary and informed, and it can be withdrawn.
Keep health information confidential and share only the minimum needed with consent or lawful justification.
Declare and manage conflicts of interest so they do not bias advice.
Work in teams with clear roles, referral and shared records.
Regulation and licensure vary by country; check the current national regulator, and remember that negligence needs duty, breach, harm and causation.

en.title: Research methods in nutrition
en.short: Study designs, dietary measurement error, bias, statistics, ethics and writing a research proposal.

sections.heading: Study designs
sections.text: Nutrition research links diet or nutrition status to health. A cross-sectional survey measures exposure and outcome at one time and shows associations. A case-control study compares past exposure in people with and without an outcome; it suits rare outcomes but depends on recall. A cohort follows people over time and estimates incidence and relative risk. A randomised controlled trial assigns the intervention by chance, balancing confounders and supporting causal inference. Systematic reviews bring studies together in a structured way; a meta-analysis pools their results statistically. Choose the design that fits the question, ethics and resources.

sections.heading: Dietary measurement
sections.text: Dietary exposure is what a person eats. Tools include 24-hour recalls, food records, food frequency questionnaires and biomarkers. All have error. Recall depends on memory; records may change eating; questionnaires depend on a fixed food list; biomarkers may reflect only recent intake. Random error varies in both directions. Systematic error, or bias, pushes results one way; underreporting is common. A missed 200 kcal snack on a recall makes estimated intake 200 kcal too low. Train interviewers, use validated tools and repeat measurements.

sections.heading: Bias and statistics
sections.text: Bias is systematic error away from the truth. Selection bias arises when the way people are chosen or kept in a study makes the sample differ from the target group. Information bias comes from wrong measurement. Confounding occurs when a third factor is linked to both exposure and outcome; income can affect diet and health, so a diet-health link may be partly confounded. Randomisation, restriction or matching can reduce confounding, and analysis can adjust for measured confounders. Statistics summarise data with means and standard deviations, or medians and interquartile ranges for skewed data. Confidence intervals give plausible ranges. A p-value is the probability of such extreme data if the null hypothesis is true, not the probability that it is true.

sections.heading: Ethics and proposal
sections.text: Research ethics requires committee approval, voluntary informed consent, confidentiality and fair selection. A proposal states the question, background, design, sample size, measurements, analysis, timeline, budget and ethics. Justify sample size; follow current national and WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Cross-sectional studies describe associations; cohorts and randomised trials support stronger causal inference.
Dietary tools all contain random and systematic error; underreporting is common.
Confounding is a third factor linked to both exposure and outcome; randomisation and adjustment reduce it.
Relative risk = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed; confidence intervals show plausible ranges.
A p-value is the probability of such extreme data if the null hypothesis is true, not the probability that it is true.
Ethical review, voluntary informed consent and a justified sample size are required before data collection.

en.title: Advanced nutrition science
en.short: Molecular nutrition, epigenetics, the gut microbiome, metabolic control and critical appraisal of research.

sections.heading: Molecular and cellular nutrition
sections.text: Molecular and cellular nutrition studies how nutrients enter cells, become metabolites and alter cell behaviour. It asks which transporters, enzymes, receptors are involved, and how signals reach the nucleus. Nutrient sensing means systems that detect energy and amino acid supply, such as AMPK and mTOR, and adjust metabolism. Metabolic regulation coordinates these pathways with hormones such as insulin and glucagon. After a meal insulin rises, cells take up glucose and storage switches on; between meals glucagon promotes release of stored fuel.

sections.heading: Nutrient genes and epigenetics
sections.text: Nutrient-gene interactions include nutrigenomics, how nutrients change gene expression, and nutrigenetics, how gene variants alter nutrient handling. Epigenetics means changes in gene activity that do not alter the DNA sequence, mainly DNA methylation, histone modification and non-coding RNA. Nutrients can supply methyl groups or cofactors for these processes. Human evidence is often observational, so a correlation between diet and a methylation mark does not prove cause. Advanced micronutrient biochemistry explains many vitamins are coenzymes or precursors and minerals as enzyme cofactors, and why bioavailability and interactions matter.

sections.heading: Microbiome and metabolic control
sections.text: The gut microbiome is the community of microorganisms in the intestine. It ferments dietary fibre to short-chain fatty acids, trains the immune system and influences host metabolism. Diet, antibiotics and environment shape it, but each person’s community differs. Metabolic regulation also involves liver, muscle and adipose tissue, which respond to nutrient and hormone signals. Microbiome findings are often associative, so avoid overclaiming.

sections.heading: Appraising primary research
sections.text: Critical reading of primary research means judging the original study, not a news report. Ask about design, randomisation, blinding, sample size, confounders, effect size and confidence intervals. Check whether the outcome is clinically meaningful and whether the study was in cells, animals or humans. When appraising a trial of a micronutrient supplement, ask whether groups were comparable, whether the marker measured matters, and whether the result has been replicated. Guidelines change and differ by country; for practice, use current WHO or national guidance. This is teaching, not medical advice.

keyPoints: Molecular nutrition links nutrient transport, cell signalling and metabolic regulation by hormones and sensors such as insulin, glucagon, AMPK and mTOR.
Nutrigenomics studies nutrient effects on gene expression; nutrigenetics studies gene variants that alter nutrient handling.
Epigenetic marks change gene activity without changing the DNA sequence, and diet can influence them.
Advanced micronutrient biochemistry explains coenzyme and cofactor roles, bioavailability and interactions.
The gut microbiome ferments fibre and interacts with immunity and metabolism, but human evidence is often associative.
Appraise primary studies for design, bias, effect size and replication, and use current WHO or national guidance for practice.

en.title: Nutritional epidemiology: measuring diet and judging evidence
en.short: How diet is measured in populations, how error is handled, and how study evidence informs policy.

sections.heading: Measuring diet
sections.text: Nutritional epidemiology studies how diet relates to health in populations. Diet is hard to measure because foods vary from day to day and people misreport. Common tools are 24-hour recalls, food frequency questionnaires (FFQs), food records and weighed intake. Each has trade-offs: recalls depend on memory, FFQs on a fixed food list, and records on literacy and burden. Measurement error is random (noise) or systematic (bias). Validation compares a tool with a stronger reference method; calibration uses validation data to correct later analyses. Biomarkers are biological measures related to intake, such as urinary nitrogen for protein or plasma carotenoids for fruit and vegetables. Few biomarkers are true recovery biomarkers, which quantitatively reflect intake over time.

sections.heading: Error and study designs
sections.text: Study designs include ecological, cross-sectional, case-control, cohort and randomised controlled trials (RCTs). Ecological studies compare groups, not individuals. Case-control studies compare people with and without an outcome. Cohorts follow people over time and can show temporality. RCTs reduce confounding but are costly and often short. Confounding is mixing with another factor. Reverse causation and selective survival also distort results. Random measurement error usually weakens associations towards no effect. If the validity coefficient (correlation between measured and true intake) is 0.5 and the true relative risk, the ratio of risk in the high-intake group to the low-intake group, is 2.0, the observed relative risk is about exp(0.5 × ln 2.0) = 1.41, not 2.0. Validation and calibration can estimate and correct this attenuation.

sections.heading: Synthesis and policy
sections.text: Systematic reviews find all relevant studies using a protocol and assess risk of bias. When the studies are similar enough, they pool results in a meta-analysis. Heterogeneity, publication bias and study quality affect conclusions. Causal inference judges whether an association is likely causal. It weighs temporality, dose-response, consistency, plausibility and experimental evidence. For policy, bodies such as WHO and national agencies judge certainty, size of effect, cost, equity and local context. A single study rarely justifies policy. Guidelines change, so check current national or WHO guidance. This summary is education, not medical advice.

keyPoints: Nutritional epidemiology measures diet in populations and links it to health.
24-hour recalls, FFQs, food records and biomarkers each carry different measurement error.
Validation compares a dietary tool with a stronger reference; calibration corrects attenuation.
Random measurement error usually pulls associations towards the null.
If the validity coefficient is 0.5 and true relative risk is 2.0, observed relative risk is about exp(0.5 × ln 2.0) = 1.41.
Systematic reviews may pool evidence in a meta-analysis, but heterogeneity, bias and context must be judged before policy use.

en.title: Nutrition policy and food systems
en.short: How food systems, governance, trade, sustainability and policy analysis shape diets and malnutrition.

sections.heading: Food systems and diets
sections.text:
A food system covers all steps from production, processing, distribution and retail to consumption and waste. It shapes diets through the food environment: the physical, economic and social conditions in which people acquire food, including markets, shops, schools and advertising.

Availability, price, convenience and marketing influence purchases. Food systems also affect nutrition through income, women’s time and food safety. Cheap, energy-dense processed foods alongside costly fresh foods can worsen diet quality.

sections.heading: Governance and policy process
sections.text:
Governance is how rules, resources and accountability are set and used by state and non-state actors. The policy process runs through agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation.

Multisectoral action matters because health, agriculture, trade, finance and education all affect diets. Instruments include standards, taxes, subsidies, school food rules and public information. Implementation depends on local capacity, data and political commitment. Nigeria has a national food and nutrition policy; check the current version, implementing plans and WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Trade, agriculture, sustainability
sections.text:
Trade and agriculture shape food supply and prices. Tariffs, subsidies, import rules and market concentration affect what is produced, imported and sold. Agricultural research, extension and market access affect smallholder incomes and food diversity.

Sustainability has environmental, economic and social dimensions: soil, water, biodiversity, climate, livelihoods and affordability. Some countries include sustainability in dietary guidelines, but the balance between health and environmental goals is debated. Policy must consider unintended effects on farmers, consumers and food security.

sections.heading: Double burden and evaluation
sections.text:
The double burden of malnutrition is the coexistence of undernutrition and overweight, obesity or diet-related disease in a population, household or person. It calls for policies that address both without worsening either. Policy analysis examines the problem, stakeholders, evidence, feasibility and likely effects.

Evaluation asks whether a policy was implemented as planned (process), whether it changed diets or health (impact), and at what cost. In a West African district, a proposed ban on advertising unhealthy foods to children would need mapping of ministries, vendors and school boards, plus a plan to measure purchases before and after.

keyPoints: Food systems shape diets through availability, price, marketing and the food environment.
Governance involves state and non-state actors, rules, resources and accountability across the policy cycle.
Trade and agriculture policies affect food supply, prices and smallholder incomes.
Sustainability has environmental, economic and social dimensions and may be included in dietary guidance.
The double burden is the coexistence of undernutrition and overweight, obesity or diet-related disease in populations, households or individuals.
Policy analysis examines problems, stakeholders and feasibility; evaluation assesses process, impact and cost.

en.title: Advanced research methods and dissertation
en.short: Advanced quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods, questionnaires, data management, ethics and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Designing the study
sections.text:
Advanced quantitative designs include cohort, case-control and randomised controlled trials; analysis may use multivariable regression to adjust for confounding, and must consider bias and statistical power.

Qualitative methods such as interviews, focus groups and ethnography explore meaning and experience; analysis is often thematic. Mixed methods combine both, for example a survey followed by interviews to explain the numbers. Integration means linking findings, not just reporting two studies. A dissertation starts with a focused question, a protocol, a realistic timeline and regular supervision.

sections.heading: Questionnaires and data
sections.text:
Questionnaire design turns concepts into measurable items. Use validated instruments where they exist, avoid leading or double-barrelled questions, and pilot the draft with a small group. Record reliability and validity.

Data management covers a codebook, unique identifiers, secure storage, backup, cleaning and an audit trail. Missing data must be reported, not hidden. Worked example: if 240 questionnaires are distributed and 180 usable ones return, the response rate is 180 ÷ 240 × 100 = 75%.

sections.heading: Ethics and approval
sections.text:
Ethics approval must be obtained before data collection. An ethics committee, also called an institutional review board, checks informed consent, confidentiality, risks and benefits, and fair selection. Vulnerable groups need extra safeguards.

Data protection law and committee requirements differ by country, so check current local and institutional rules. Keep approvals, consent forms and amendments on file.

sections.heading: Conducting and writing
sections.text:
Conduct the study to the approved protocol: pilot, recruit, monitor, document decisions and analyse according to a pre-specified plan. In mixed methods, show how strands are integrated.

Write the dissertation in a clear structure: introduction and question, literature review, methods, results, discussion, limitations and conclusion. Report methods fully enough for another researcher to repeat them, and follow relevant reporting guidelines. The viva, or oral defence, tests your choices, not your memory.

keyPoints: Advanced quantitative designs estimate effects and must address bias, confounding and statistical power.
Qualitative methods explore meaning; mixed methods integrate both strands.
Pilot questionnaires and avoid leading or double-barrelled items.
Keep a codebook, unique identifiers, secure backup and an audit trail.
Obtain ethics approval before data collection; rules differ by country.
Response rate = usable returns ÷ questionnaires distributed × 100.
